templates.pattern: A solar panel faces a surface tilted at [TILT]° from horizontal. The horizontal irradiance is [GH] W/m² and the angle of incidence is [AOI]°. Calculate irradiance on the tilted surface (W/m²) using: G_tilt = GH × cos(AOI) / cos(TILT). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Irradiance on tilted surface: G_tilt = GH × cos(AOI) / cos(tilt)
= [GH] × cos([AOI]°) / cos([TILT]°)
= [RESULT] W/m²

Tilting panels towards the equator (south in northern hemisphere) increases the annual energy yield by 10–20% compared to horizontal mounting. The optimal tilt angle roughly equals the site's latitude. Tracking systems can further boost yield by 20–35%.

templates.pattern: A wind mast records wind speed [V1] m/s at [H1] m height. Using the wind shear power law, calculate the wind speed (m/s) at hub height [H2] m with roughness exponent α = [ALPHA] (expressed as a decimal, e.g. 0.14). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Wind Shear Power Law: V2 = V1 × (H2/H1)^α
= [V1] × ([H2]/[H1])^([ALPHA]/100)
= [RESULT] m/s

Wind speed increases with height due to reduced surface friction. The roughness exponent α varies: open sea ~0.11, open grassland ~0.14, farmland ~0.20, suburban ~0.25, urban ~0.33. This is why modern turbines use taller towers (100–150 m) to capture faster, more consistent winds.

templates.pattern: A wind turbine has a rotor diameter of [D] m operating in wind speed [V] m/s with air density ρ = 1.225 kg/m³. Its actual power output is [PACT] kW. Calculate the turbine's power coefficient Cp as a fraction of the theoretical maximum. Round to 4 decimal places. (Theoretical max P = 0.5 × ρ × A × v³, where A = π(D/2)².)
templates.explanation:
Power Coefficient Cp = Actual Power ÷ Theoretical Wind Power
Theoretical P = 0.5 × 1.225 × π×(D/2)² × v³
Cp = [PACT]×10³ ÷ (0.5 × 1.225 × π × ([D]/2)² × [V]³)
= [RESULT]

The Betz limit caps Cp at 16/27 ≈ 0.593. Modern turbines achieve Cp of 0.45–0.50. Values above 0.593 are physically impossible — they would indicate an error in measurement or calculation.

templates.pattern: A wind farm has an installed capacity of [CAP] MW, a capacity factor of [CF]%, and operates for [LIFE] years. Calculate the total annual energy yield (GWh/yr) and the lifetime energy yield (GWh).
templates.explanation:
Annual Energy Yield = Capacity × Capacity Factor × Hours per year
= [CAP] MW × ([CF]/100) × 8760 hr/yr
= [RESULT] GWh/yr

Lifetime yield = [RESULT] × [LIFE] = [RESULT*LIFE] GWh

Annual energy yield drives revenue forecasting and is the denominator in LCOE calculations. Offshore wind farms (~40% CF) generate roughly twice the annual energy of equivalent onshore solar farms (~20% CF) for the same installed capacity.

templates.pattern: A solar farm must generate [TARGET] GWh/yr. Panels have efficiency [EFF]% and the site receives average irradiance of [IRRAD] kWh/m²/day. Calculate the land area required (hectares), assuming a ground coverage ratio of [GCR]%. Round to 1 decimal place.
templates.explanation:
Panel area = Target energy ÷ (efficiency × annual irradiance)
Annual irradiance = [IRRAD] × 365 kWh/m²/yr
Panel area = [TARGET]×10⁹ Wh ÷ ([EFF]/100 × [IRRAD]×365×1000 Wh/m²)
Land area = Panel area ÷ (GCR/100) ÷ 10000 m²/ha
= [RESULT] hectares

Ground Coverage Ratio (GCR) accounts for spacing between panel rows needed to avoid self-shading. Typical utility-scale solar farms require 1–2 hectares per MW of installed capacity.

templates.pattern: A region needs [PTARGET] MW of offshore wind power. Each turbine is rated at [PTURB] MW and has a capacity factor of [CF]%. How many turbines are needed to reliably meet the target on average? Round up to the nearest whole turbine.
templates.explanation:
Effective output per turbine = Rated power × Capacity Factor
= [PTURB] × [CF]/100 MW average
Number of turbines = Target ÷ Effective output per turbine
= [PTARGET] ÷ ([PTURB] × [CF]/100)
= [RESULT] turbines (rounded up)

Rounding up ensures the fleet meets the target on average. In practice, additional turbines are included as reserve margin to account for maintenance downtime and variability.

templates.pattern: A battery bank has a capacity of [CAP] kWh. It is charged with [IN] kWh and discharged. The round-trip efficiency is [EFF]%. Calculate the usable energy delivered (kWh) on discharge.
templates.explanation:
Usable Energy = Energy In × Round-trip Efficiency
= [IN] kWh × ([EFF]/100)
= [RESULT] kWh

Round-trip efficiency (RTE) accounts for losses during both charge and discharge. Lithium-ion batteries: RTE 90–98%; pumped hydro: 70–85%; vanadium flow batteries: 65–80%; hydrogen (P2G2P): 25–40%. RTE losses directly increase the effective cost of stored energy.

templates.pattern: A wind farm is connected to the grid via a cable with resistance [R] ohms. The farm exports current [I] amps at [V] kV. Calculate the transmission power loss (kW) using P_loss = I² × R.
templates.explanation:
Transmission Power Loss = I² × R
= [I]² × [R] W
= [RESULT] kW

Ohmic (resistive) losses increase with the square of current. This is why electricity is transmitted at high voltages (lower current for the same power). High-voltage DC (HVDC) cables are preferred for long offshore wind connections due to lower losses compared to AC cables.

templates.pattern: A renewable energy plant generates [ENERGY] MWh/yr and displaces electricity from a gas power station with a carbon intensity of [CI] gCO₂/kWh. Calculate the annual carbon saving (tonnes CO₂/yr).
templates.explanation:
Carbon Saving = Energy Generated × Carbon Intensity of Displaced Generation
= [ENERGY] MWh × [CI] gCO₂/kWh × 1000 kWh/MWh ÷ 10⁶ g/tonne
= [RESULT] tonnes CO₂/yr

Carbon intensity varies by fuel and technology: gas CCGT ~350–450 gCO₂/kWh, coal ~820 gCO₂/kWh, nuclear ~12 gCO₂/kWh, wind ~7–15 gCO₂/kWh (lifecycle). Grid average carbon intensity falls as more renewables are added.

templates.pattern: A wind project costs £[CAPEX] million upfront. It generates annual revenue of £[REV] million for [LIFE] years. Using a discount rate of [DR]%, calculate the Net Present Value (NPV) in £ million: NPV = −CAPEX + REV × (1 − (1+DR/100)^(−LIFE)) / (DR/100). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
NPV = −CAPEX + REV × annuity factor
Annuity factor = (1 − (1+r)^(−n)) / r  where r = [DR]/100, n = [LIFE]
NPV = −[CAPEX] + [REV] × (1 − (1+[DR]/100)^(−[LIFE])) / ([DR]/100)
= £[RESULT] million

Positive NPV means the project creates value. The discount rate reflects opportunity cost of capital and project risk. Renewable energy projects typically require NPV > 0 at discount rates of 5–10% to attract private investment.
